strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a practical clinical NLP bottleneck: access to annotated clinical text. Its 8,767 examples cover 14 SBDH categories plus pain, with spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. The resource contribution is valuable independently of methodological novelty.

The experiments support the central claim that synthetic pretraining can improve downstream classification. Prompt-based RoBERTa improves from 55.64 to 91.11 macro-F on MIMIC-SBDH-aligned, and standard RoBERTa improves from 72.38 to 80.71 on VA-SBDH. Multiple architectures, three-run reporting, category-level results, and training-size experiments strengthen this evidence.

The expert audit is substantial: two experienced annotators review all 1,755 synthetic test examples, correct annotations, add omissions, and assess rationales. Publishing the reviewed test set and detailed error analysis increases the resource's usefulness.

The manuscript documents the generator version, generation prompt, 45 seed examples, filtering procedure, category mappings, and training configurations, and provides a repository link. These materials support reuse and make the core resource contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The benefits are less uniform than the abstract's claim that models consistently outperform their counterparts. Full-data encoder NER results are essentially unchanged; VA classification gains are negligible or negative for some Mamba and Llama settings. The large T5 NER improvement starts from an unstable baseline of 25.44 ± 18.24 macro-F, whereas FLAN-T5 gains 1.41 points. These results support conditional augmentation benefits rather than broadly reliable improvements.

The experiments do not adequately distinguish benefits of synthetic content from additional optimization and improved class coverage. The matched-training comparison against MIMIC pretraining is useful, but its four-category coverage differs from Synth-SBDH's broader coverage. Class-balanced sampling, loss reweighting, or extended target-only training would strengthen the interpretation of the headline gains. Housing insecurity has only 18 test positives, so variation across training seeds does not capture uncertainty from the small evaluation sample.

Annotation quality requires qualified interpretation. The audit corrects 286 annotations, discards 142, and adds 581 missing annotations. Moreover, review guidelines differ from the generation instructions: Appendix E.2 excludes some context-specific stress mentions that seed examples label positively, and introduces an 'unclear' temporal value. Such changes complicate interpreting disagreement purely as generator error. All downstream tasks retain only presence-positive annotations and do not evaluate temporal extraction, leaving important advertised attributes insufficiently validated.

The reasoning-distillation claim exceeds the evidence. DSS improves macro-F by only 0.66 points for T5 and 0.58 for FLAN-T5, with the latter nonsignificant at the reported P=0.36. Evaluation uses synthetic text only, and there is no control using shuffled rationales or comparable auxiliary supervision. This demonstrates limited auxiliary-task benefits, without establishing transferable reasoning capability.

Generalizability is demonstrated under target-domain supervision: models are fine-tuned on each real dataset before evaluation. This does not establish performance at an unseen hospital without adaptation. The synthetic snippets also average only 13.7 words, versus 35.13 and 47.43 in the real datasets, limiting conclusions about realistic clinical-document complexity.

Reproducibility and reporting need clarification. VA-SBDH is private, and exact downstream prompt templates/verbalizers and generation decoding settings are not specified in the manuscript. The reported synthetic split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767. Table 14 also repeats several ClinicalMamba statistics from Table 3 for Llama 3.2 and should be checked. These issues, together with the limited scope of the stronger claims, constrain the main-conference case.
